paragraphs: Here's the big idea, friend: God is the Potter, and we are the clay. Isaiah says it's upside down when the pottery says of the potter, "He has no understanding" (Isaiah 29:16). Hiding plans from the LORD in the dark, asking "Who sees us, and who will know?" (Isaiah 29:15), is the same mistake. I tried hiding a burnt batch once, and the whole planet still knew, so I'm not the one to try hiding anything from the God who made me.

But look at where the passage lands, because it does NOT end in the dark. The LORD promises that the deaf will hear, the blind will see, and the humble and the poor will "increase their joy in the LORD" (Isaiah 29:18, 19). The ruthless, the mockers and the ones with false charges will not have the last word (Isaiah 29:20, 21). The One who sees everything also sees the people who got treated unfairly, and He is the One who sets things right.

And the last verses might be my favorite. The LORD calls Jacob's children "the work of My hands" (Isaiah 29:23), so the Potter is proud of what He made. Even "the wayward in spirit will come to understanding, and those who grumble will accept instruction" (Isaiah 29:24). So, baker, when you catch yourself grumbling, or sure you know better than the Potter, there's good news: He's patient with clay, and He is still shaping you.
